Discussion

Although prior literature suggests that extremist groups are characterized by stronger ties and greater cohesion than moderate ones (Whitehouse et al., 2014), our findings run counter to these expectations. Frequency of meetings, perceived importance of the group, and closeness with friends were all higher in moderate groups and there were no differences in identity fusion. Several explanations could account for this pattern. Moderate groups, by operating within socially accepted boundaries, may offer more opportunities for sustained interpersonal contact, facilitating deeper social bonding. Their broader memberships may also allow individuals to form selective, high-quality relationships. In contrast, radical organizations tend to be smaller and more insular, which may limit opportunities to cultivate strong ties and require members to maintain relationships based on availability.

Radical groups may also be more task-focused-drawing people together primarily because of shared goals and limiting their interactions to organizational matters. Our exploratory analyses offer some support for this idea, as members of the radical group seemed to value their friends' commitment to the group's goals more than members of the moderate group, conditioning their sense of closeness on this commitment. This could suggest that whereas moderate groups prioritize personal relationships, radical groups may emphasize task completion. This distinction resembles the classic research that distinguishes between taskoriented and relationship-oriented group structures (Slater, 1955). Task-oriented groups may be a better model for extreme organizations, where personal bonds yield to the pursuit of mission-related goals and social ties are built on instrumental contribution to group goals. Conversely, moderate organizations may resemble relationship-oriented systems, prioritizing interpersonal bonds and intimacy. This framework may help explain why members of moderate groups reported stronger overall social ties, while members of radical groups conditioned closeness more strongly on perceived commitment. Still, it is worth noting that radical groups were not, on average, perceived as more committed to their goals than moderate groups suggesting that this hypothesis warrants further examination.

We also found that perceptions of more vs. less violent friends varied between groups.

Within the radical organization, higher levels of friend's violent extremism were associated with closer relationships and were interpreted as signs of stronger group commitment. These findings support the idea that the meaning of violence is context-dependent: in some contexts it can be positively valued as an expression of dedication to a cause. Contrary to expectations, we did not find evidence that more violent friends were evaluated more negatively or kept at greater distance in the moderate organization. However, such individuals may have been excluded from members' close social networks in the first place.

Importantly, we operationalized social context both through organizational membership and personal networks. Although past research shows that both types of context are related to personal violence (Holman, 2016; Jasko et al., 2017 Jasko et al., , 2020;; Dahl & van Zalk, 2014), these influences can sometimes compete or even contradict one another. Our results suggest that the organizational, rather than the interpersonal, level moderates reactions to violent close others. Several organizational factors might also explain these patterns. Radical organizations may socialize members into accepting violence through ideological narratives, leadership practices, and internal norms. Interestingly, we found no significant differences in norm tightness between the organizations and members of moderate groups cared more about what their friends thought of them than those in radical groups. Together these results challenge the assumption that more radical organizations exert stronger normative pressure on their members.

Limitations

One limitation of our study was its correlational design. We did not capture whether participants formed friendships with violent members before or after they displayed violent tendencies, making it difficult to determine whether violence causally shaped closeness. The implications for deradicalization strategies would vary depending on the underlying mechanism, necessitating further research, ideally through longitudinal studies.

Because our study examined only two organizations at a single point in time, organization-level idiosyncrasies may have influenced the observed effects. There may be some unmeasured differences between these organizations that extend beyond their stance on violence. Cultural factors could influence how social ties are formed and maintained in these groups, making it difficult to generalize findings across the broader context of Indonesian Islamism.

Although we observed consistent differences in violent extremism between the groups, even members of Jemaah Islamiyah did not report extremely high levels of extremism. It is possible that the most extreme members may have been unwilling to participate due to security concerns. Consequently, questions remain about the extent to which our results would generalize to, or even become amplified in, more highly radicalized groups. At the same time, this pattern appears consistent with JI's organizational position around the time of data collection (IPAC, 2021). Indeed, in 2024 the organization formally dissolved, publicly disavowing violence. This trajectory may reflect the perceived ineffectiveness of violence relative to peaceful strategies in achieving political goals. Such a decline would be consistent with the logic proposed in the present paper: if radical groups are more task-oriented, assessments of effectiveness may play a stronger role in shaping engagement than in moderate groups.

More generally, our findings suggest that the "radicals'-camaraderie" hypothesis may be overgeneralized and in need of a finer differentiation between commitment to the group's objectives and the quality of interpersonal ties in radical and moderate groups.
